modern_osis:
Original heading

The Lord is to be praised for his works.

Praise for God's works and covenant faithfulness

The psalmist resolved to praise God himself.

Our personal example should agree with what we encourage other people to do.

God's works are the proper subject of praise, including his providence toward the world, his church and individual people.

Although the Lord's works are many, they can be spoken of as one work, because all the different events of Providence contribute to a single wise purpose.

When we examine his works humbly and diligently, we discover that they are just and holy.

Of all God's works, his forgiveness of sin is the most wonderful, and we should remember it for his glory.

God never forgets his covenant.

He has always remembered it and always will.

His works of Providence follow the truth of his promises and prophecies.

They are therefore true.

Because he has the right to govern the earth as he chooses, they are also righteous.

The same is true of his work of grace in human hearts.

Every divine command is sure.

All God's commandments were fulfilled by Christ, and they remain our standard of conduct in him.

The Lord redeemed his people from Egypt and delivered them repeatedly afterward.

These rescues pictured the greater redemption accomplished by Jesus Christ in the fullness of time.

In that redemption, everlasting righteousness shines together with boundless mercy.

No one is truly wise without the fear of the Lord.

That reverence leads to repentance, faith in Christ, vigilance and obedience.

Those who live this way possess real understanding, even if they are poor, lack formal learning or are despised by others.
classic_reading:
[Ps.111.1]
Chapter 111
The Lord is to be praised for his works.
--The psalmist resolves to praise God himself. Our exhortations and our examples should agree together. He recommends the works of the Lord, as the proper subject, when we are praising him; and the dealings of his providence toward the world, the church, and particular persons. All the works of the Lord are spoken of as one, it is his work; so admirably do all the dispensations of his providence centre in one design. The works of God, humbly and diligently sought into, shall all be found just and holy. God's pardoning sin is the most wonderful of all his works, and ought to be remembered to his glory. He will ever be mindful of his covenant; he has ever been so, and he ever will be so. His works of providence were done according to the truth of the Divine promises and prophecies, and so were verity, or truth; and by him who has a right to dispose of the earth as he pleases, and so are judgment, or righteous: and this holds good of the work of grace upon the heart of man, ver. #(7-8). All God's commandments are sure; all have been fulfilled by Christ, and remain with him for a rule of walk and conversation to us. He sent redemption unto his people, out of Egypt at first, and often afterwards; and these were typical of the great redemption, which in the fulness of time was to be wrought out by the Lord Jesus. Here his everlasting righteousness shines forth in union with his boundless mercy. No man is wise who does not fear the Lord; no man acts wisely except as influenced by that fear. This fear will lead to repentance, to faith in Christ, to watchfulness and obedience. Such persons are of a good understanding, however poor, unlearned, or despised.

modern_osis:
Original heading

The blessedness of the righteous.

The blessing of trusting and fearing God

We should praise the Lord because there are people in the world who fear and serve him, and because they are happy through his grace alone.

Their fear is not the terror that love drives away.

It is the reverence that love produces: a desire not to offend the One they love.

This fear belongs together with trust.

When the Holy Spirit touches a heart, it turns quickly toward God, like a compass needle touched by a magnet.

It does so with loving reverence and awe.

God has stored up blessings for the faithful and their descendants.

He gives them genuine riches, together with as much earthly property as is truly beneficial to them.

Even during their darkest troubles, hope and peace can dawn within them, and timely help can turn grief into joy.

Their Lord teaches them to be compassionate, kind and fair in every relationship.

They use good judgment so that their generosity may do the greatest good.

Envy and slander may temporarily hide their true character, but they will be remembered with lasting honor.

They do not need to fear every alarming report.

Their hearts can become stable.

True believers seek to keep their thoughts fixed upon God, making their hearts calm.

He has promised both reasons for confidence and grace to exercise it.

Trusting him is the firmest foundation for the heart.

Human hearts cannot settle with complete satisfaction anywhere except in the truth of God.

Faith gives them a stable footing and patience to wait for the appointed outcome.

Compare this with the distress of the wicked.

They envy the happiness of God's people.

But their desires are entirely bound to worldly pleasure and the flesh.

When these perish, their joy perishes too.

The blessings of the gospel are spiritual and everlasting.

They belong to Christ's church through Christ its Head, who is the example of every righteous life and the giver of all grace.
classic_reading:
[Ps.112.1]
Chapter 112
The blessedness of the righteous.
--We have to praise the Lord that there are a people in the world, who fear him and serve him, and that they are a happy people; which is owing entirely to his grace. Their fear is not that which love casts out, but that which love brings in. It follows and flows from love. It is a fear to offend. This is both fear and trust. The heart touched by the Spirit of God, as the needle touched with the loadstone, turns direct and speedily to God, yet still with trembling, being filled with this holy fear. Blessings are laid up for the faithful and their children's children; and true riches are bestowed on them, with as much of this world's possessions as is profitable for them. In the darkest hours of affliction and trial, the light of hope and peace will spring up within them, and seasonable relief shall turn mourning into joy. From their Lord's example they learn to be kind and full of compassion, as well as just in all their dealings; they use discretion, that they may be liberal in that manner which appears most likely to do good. Envy and slander may for a time hide their true characters here, but they shall be had in everlasting remembrance. They need not fear evil tidings. A good man shall have a settled spirit. And it is the endeavour of true believers to keep their minds stayed upon God, and so to keep them calm and undisturbed; and God has promised them both cause to do so, and grace to do so. Trusting in the Lord is the best and surest way of establishing the heart. The heart of man cannot fix any where with satisfaction, but in the truth of God, and there it finds firm footing. And those whose hearts are established by faith, will patiently wait till they gain their point. Compare all this with the vexation of sinners. The happiness of the saints is the envy of the wicked. The desire of the wicked shall perish; their desire was wholly to the world and the flesh, therefore when these perish, their joy is gone. But the blessings of the gospel are spiritual and eternal, and are conferred upon the members of the Christian church, through Christ their Head, who is the Pattern of all righteousness, and the Giver of all grace.

modern_osis:
Original heading

An exhortation to praise God.

Praise the God who raises the lowly

God receives praise from his own people.

They have special reason to praise him because they know him as his servants and experience so much of his kindness.

Speaking well of such a Master is a joyful and pleasant task.

His name ought to be praised everywhere, from east to west.

It should be praised throughout the world, though this is not yet the case.

One day all nations will come to worship him.

God is exalted above every blessing and praise we can offer.

We should ask with holy amazement: Who is like the Lord our God?

How astonishing that he stoops to observe the affairs of the earth!

How much more astonishing that the Son of God came from heaven to earth and took our human nature to seek and save the lost!

He loved guilty sinners so greatly that he became human to ransom their souls.

Sometimes the Lord displays his wisdom and power by choosing people whom nobody would have considered capable of important work—not even the people themselves.

He called fishermen to become fishers of people.

That is his customary way in the kingdom of grace.

He receives people who are naturally beggars and even traitors, makes them his friends and children, and gives them honor as kings and priests.

He counts them among the princes of his chosen people.

All our comforts come from him.

They can be especially welcome after a long delay, when we had given up expecting them.

Let us pray that countries still barren of gospel fruit will soon become fruitful and that many converts will join in praising the Lord.

The apostles were sent from fishing to be fishers of men. And this is God's constant method in his kingdom of grace. He takes men, by nature beggars, and even traitors, to be his favourites, his children, kings and priests unto him; and numbers them with the princes of his chosen people. He gives us all our comforts, which are generally the more welcome when long delayed, and no longer expected. Let us pray that those lands which are yet barren, may speedily become fruitful, and produce many converts to join in praising the Lord.

modern_osis:
Original heading

An exhortation to fear God.

God's presence in redemption and renewal

We should recognize God's power and goodness in delivering Israel.

Those events point toward the far greater wonder of our redemption through Christ.

They should encourage us and others to trust God in the greatest difficulties.

When Christ comes to save his people, he releases them from sin and Satan's power.

He separates them from a godless world, forms them into his own people and becomes their King.

No sea or river Jordan is too wide or deep for the Lord.

When the appointed time comes, he can divide it and drive its waters back.

The same power established the Christian church in the world.

Satan and the powers of idolatry trembled before it.

But the most personal application concerns the Spirit's work within a heart.

What turns the current of a regenerated person's affections?

Why do sinful desires and corrupt habits retreat?

How are prejudices removed and an entire person made new?

It happens through the presence of God's Spirit.

At the Lord's presence even mountains and the whole earth may tremble, for creation has been placed under a curse through human sin.

God both protected and provided for Israel through miracles.

One was the stream of water flowing from a hard rock.

That rock pointed to Christ.

The Son of God, the Rock of Ages, gave himself in death to open a fountain that washes away sins and supplies believers with water of life and consolation.

No promised blessing is too great for them to expect from his love.

But sinners should fear their righteous and holy Judge.

Let us prepare now to meet God so we may stand before him with confidence when he comes.

Chapter 114
An exhortation to fear God.

When Christ comes for the salvation of his people , he redeems them from the power of sin and Satan, separates them from an ungodly world, forms them to be his people, and becomes their King. Glory belongs to God alone (verses 1–8)

We must never appeal to our own merit in our prayers or praises.

Any good we accomplish comes from God's grace, and every good thing we possess is a gift of his free mercy.

He therefore deserves all the praise.

When we seek mercy and wrestle in prayer, we should look for encouragement in God alone.

Lord, act for us—not so that we may take the credit or comfort for ourselves, but so that your mercy and faithfulness will receive the glory.

The gods of the nations are lifeless things, made by human hands.

A painter, a sculptor or a craftsman cannot give life to an image and therefore cannot give it sensation or knowledge.

The psalm shows the folly of those who worship such idols.

Trust, praise and the living God (verses 9–18)

Trusting lifeless images is foolish.

Trusting the living God is wise, because he is help and shield to everyone who relies on him.

True reverence for God can be joined to cheerful confidence in him.

Those who respect his word may trust it.

He has always proved faithful.

The greatest people need his blessing.

He will not deny his blessing to the humblest person who fears him.

God's blessing brings growth, especially spiritual growth.

We should praise the Lord for his wide generosity in giving the earth to human beings for their use.

After their souls are released from the burdens of their mortal bodies, faithful believers continue praising him.

But a dead body cannot praise God.

Death ends our opportunity to glorify him through work and struggle in this present world.

Other people have died, bringing their earthly service to an end.

We should therefore strive to do more for God while we still live.

We should also encourage others to praise him, even after we ourselves are gone.

Lord, you alone deserve our faith and love.

Help us praise you while living and as we die.

May your name be first and last upon our lips, and may its sweetness refresh our souls forever.

Loving the God who saves (verses 1–9)

We have many reasons to love the Lord, but his kindness affects us especially deeply when he rescues us from terrible trouble.

When sinners become aware of their true condition and fear that God's righteous judgment will destroy them, they experience great sorrow and distress.

Let them call upon the Lord to save their souls.

They will find him gracious and faithful to his promises.

Neither a person's former ignorance nor guilt will prevent salvation when that person trusts the Lord.

We should describe God according to our experience of him.

Have we ever found him anything other than just and good?

Only his mercy prevents us from being consumed.

Let those who labor and carry heavy burdens come to him and receive rest for their souls.

If they wander from that rest, let them return quickly, remembering how generous he has been.

We should live with a continual sense of being in his presence.

It is a great mercy to be kept from being swallowed up by overwhelming sorrow.

It is also a mercy when God upholds our right hand so that temptation does not overpower and overthrow us.

When we enter the heavenly rest, deliverance from sin and sorrow will be complete.

We will see the Lord's glory and walk in his presence with a joy we cannot yet imagine.

Gratitude expressed in service and devotion (verses 10–19)

During trouble, it is often best to be quiet because pain may lead us to speak rashly.

Genuine faith may coexist with struggles of unbelief, but faith will eventually prevail.

When we humble ourselves for distrusting God's promises, we can experience his faithfulness.

What can a forgiven sinner, or anyone rescued from danger, offer in return for the Lord's goodness?

We cannot benefit him in any way.

Even our very best offering is unworthy of his acceptance.

Yet we should dedicate ourselves and all we possess to him.

The psalmist resolves to take the cup of salvation.

This includes the drink offering appointed by the law as a thankful response to God.

It also includes receiving the cup of affliction: bitter suffering can be sanctified to God's people and become a means of spiritual healing.

And it includes the cup of consolation: accepting God's comforts as gifts from his hand and recognizing his love in blessings enjoyed now as well as in the coming inheritance.

The psalmist chooses to be God's servant regardless of whom others serve.

People may become servants in two ways.

First, through birth: the psalmist was born in the Lord's household as the son of one of his servants.

Having godly parents is a great mercy.

Second, through redemption: God broke his bonds and rescued him.

Those loosened bonds made him more firmly devoted to his Redeemer.

Doing good is a sacrifice that pleases God, and it must accompany thanksgiving.

Why would we offer the Lord something that costs us nothing?

The psalmist resolved to fulfill his vows immediately.

He would do so publicly, not to boast, but to show that he was not ashamed of God's service and to invite others to join in.

Such are God's genuine saints, whose lives and deaths will bring him glory.

We should deem ourselves bound to walk as in his presence. It is a great mercy to be kept from being swallowed up with over-much sorrow. It is a great mercy for God to hold us by the right hand, so that we are not overcome and overthrown by a temptation. When troubled, we do best to hold our peace, for we are apt to speak unadvisedly. Our best is unworthy of his acceptance; yet we ought to devote ourselves and all we have to his service. I will take the cup of salvation; I will offer the drink-offerings appointed by the law, in token of thankfulness to God, and rejoice in God's goodness to me. I will receive the cup of affliction; that cup, that bitter cup, which is sanctified to the saints, so that to them it is a cup of salvation; it is a means of spiritual health. The psalmist will pay his vows now; he will not delay the payment: publicly, not to make a boast, but to show he is not ashamed of God's service, and to invite others to join him. Such are true saints of God, in whose lives and deaths he will be glorified.

Original heading

All people called upon to praise God.

All nations invited to praise the Lord

This psalm solemnly calls every nation to praise the Lord and gives them reasons to do so.

We soon grow tired of doing good if we do not keep devout and loving affection for God alive within us.

The spiritual sacrifice of praise needs to be kindled and kept burning.

This is a gospel psalm.

The apostle Paul quotes it in Romans 15:11, showing that the gospel was intended to be preached among the nations and would be welcomed by them.

For many centuries, God was known and praised especially within Judah.

The nations outside Israel were not yet receiving this call in the same way.

But Christ's gospel has been commanded to be preached to all nations.

Through him, people who were once far away have been brought near.

We ourselves are among the people to whom the Holy Spirit speaks through this psalm, inviting us to join God's ancient people in praise.

Grace has therefore abounded toward multitudes of sinners who were heading toward destruction.

Let us receive God's gracious invitation and pray for the day when every nation on earth will proclaim his praise.

Bless the Lord for the unsearchable riches of gospel grace.

Trusting God's mercy in every trial (verses 1–18)

The psalmist's account of his suffering is especially applicable to Jesus Christ.

Many hated Christ without cause.

The Lord also subjected him to severe suffering, bruising and grieving him so that through his wounds we might be healed.

At times God strengthens his people when he is not yet their delight.

They may receive spiritual support without the immediate pleasure of spiritual comfort.

Believers can find abundant reasons for praise whether they look back to the Lord's everlasting kindness and mercy or forward to his promised blessings.

Every answer to prayer reminds us that the Lord is on our side.

Therefore we need not be ruled by fear of what other people can do.

We must faithfully perform our duties toward everyone and trust God alone to accept and bless our service.

Seek to live so that you can declare God's works and encourage others to serve and trust him.

This confidence also characterized the triumphs of the Son of David, who knew the Lord's purpose would prosper in his hands.

Christ, the rejected stone who became the cornerstone (verses 19–29)

Even ancient believers who saw Christ's coming from a great distance had reason to praise God in anticipation.

The prophecy about the stone rejected by the builders (verses 22 and 23) may refer in part to David's promotion, but it points principally toward Christ.

First, his humiliation: he is the stone the builders rejected.

They attempted to continue their work without him, and their rejection brought their own ruin.

Those who reject Christ are themselves rejected by God.

Second, his exaltation: Christ became the chief cornerstone of the foundation.

He is also the final topstone that completes the building and therefore deserves preeminence in everything.

His name is Wonderful, and the redemption he accomplished is the greatest of God's marvelous works.

We should rejoice in the Lord's day, not only because he has appointed it, but because it celebrates Christ becoming the Head.

Sabbaths ought to be joyful days, giving us a foretaste of heaven.

Let this Savior be my Savior and Ruler.

May my soul prosper and be in health through the peace and righteousness of his reign.

May he give me victory over desires that fight against my soul and, through grace, bring my heart under his rule.

The duties he commands come with true light.

Our response to the privilege of redemption must include sacrifices of gratitude.

These are not bodies killed upon an altar, but ourselves as living sacrifices, bound to the altar in grateful dedication to God.

They also include spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise in which our hearts sincerely participate.

The psalmist praises the Lord and invites everyone nearby to give thanks for the good news of great joy: there is a Redeemer, Christ the Lord.

In him the covenant of grace is secure and everlasting.

God is sometimes the strength of his people, when he is not their song; they have spiritual supports, though they want spiritual delights. Whether the believer traces back his comfort to the everlasting goodness and mercy of God, or whether he looks forward to the blessing secured to him, he will find abundant cause for joy and praise. Every answer to our prayers is an evidence that the Lord is on our side; and then we need not fear what man can do unto us; we should conscientiously do our duty to all, and trust in him alone to accept and bless us. Let us seek to live to declare the works of God, and to encourage others to serve him and trust in him. Such were the triumphs of the Son of David, in the assurance that the good pleasure of the Lord should prosper in his hand.

Verses 19-29
Those who saw Christ's day at so great a distance, saw cause to praise God for the prospect. The prophecy, ver. #(22-23), may refer to David's preferment; but principally to Christ. 1. His humiliation; he is the Stone which the builders refused: they would go on in their building without him. This proved the ruin of those who thus made light of him. Rejecters of Christ are rejected of God. 2. His exaltation; he is the chief Cornerstone in the foundation. He is the chief Top-stone, in whom the building is completed, who must, in all things, have the pre-eminence. Christ's name is Wonderful; and the redemption he wrought out is the most amazing of all God's wondrous works. Sabbath days ought to be rejoicing days, then they are to us as the days of heaven. Let this Saviour be my Saviour, my Ruler. The duty which the Lord has made, brings light with it, true light. The duty this privilege calls for, is here set forth; the sacrifices we are to offer to God in gratitude for redeeming love, are ourselves; not to be slain upon the altar, but living sacrifices, to be bound to the altar; spiritual sacrifices of prayer and praise, in which our hearts must be engaged. The psalmist praises God, and calls upon all about him to give thanks to God for the glad tidings of great joy to all people, that there is a Redeemer, even Christ the Lord. In him the covenant of grace is made sure and everlasting.

Original authorial introduction

The chief purpose of this psalm is to honor God's law and show its greatness.

Henry identifies ten terms used here for divine revelation, each teaching us something about what the Lord expects of us and what we may expect from him.

1. His law is enacted by God, our Sovereign. 2. His way describes the rule of his Providence. 3. His testimonies are solemnly declared to the world. 4. His commandments are given with divine authority. 5. His precepts are binding rather than optional. 6. His word or saying declares God's mind. 7. His judgments proceed from infinite wisdom. 8. His righteousness is the standard of what is right. 9. His statutes remain continually binding. 10. His truth or faithfulness endures forever.

The original secondary witness presents this introduction before the first exposition, without assigning it to an invented verse section.

Wholehearted obedience through grace (verses 1–8)

This psalm can be read as the spiritual experience of a believer.

Our attitudes, desires and affections come from the Holy Spirit only to the extent that they agree with what the psalm expresses.

God's forgiving mercy in Christ is the only source of lasting happiness for a sinner.

The happiest people are those preserved most carefully from sin's pollution, who believe the Lord's testimony and rely on his promises.

A heart divided between God and the world is in a dangerous condition.

The saints do not claim to have no remaining sin. They know there are many things within them that hinder obedience.

Yet they do not willingly embrace the wickedness that would draw them entirely away from the Lord's paths.

The tempter would persuade people that obeying God's word is merely a personal choice.

But a godly person's desires and prayers agree with God's will and commands.

We cannot expect obedience in one duty to purchase permission for disobedience in others.

Such hypocrisy will be exposed: if its shame is not faced in this life, everlasting shame will be its portion.

The psalmist wanted to learn God's law and give him glory.

Believers know that if God abandons them to themselves, the tempter will be too strong.

God's word treasured in the heart (verses 9–16)

To the corruption inherited from Adam, all people have added their own actual sins.

Young people may ruin themselves by living without any standard or by choosing a false one.

Let them use Scripture as their rule of life.

Distrusting our own wisdom and strength and depending upon God show a sincere desire for holiness.

God's word is a treasure worth storing.

Its safest resting place is within the heart.

We then answer sin's demands with God's precepts, its attractions with his promises, and its threats with his warnings.

Ask the Lord to teach his statutes, so that sharing in his holiness we may also share in his blessedness.

Those nourished by the bread of life ought to feed others through their words.

God's commands lead us toward the unsearchable riches of Christ.

But meditation is not truly useful unless good thoughts produce good actions.

We should not merely consider God's statutes, but practice them gladly.

Test the sincerity of obedience by examining what motivates it, and test love for God by whether his appointed duties are performed cheerfully.

Strangers on earth, sustained by God's counsel (verses 17–24)

If God judged us with complete strictness, every one of us would perish.

Our lives should therefore be spent in his service.

We find true life through keeping his word.

To see the wonders of God's law and gospel, we must ask for understanding through his Spirit's light.

Believers know they are strangers on earth.

They fear losing their way or forfeiting comfort through disobedience.

A sanctified soul hungers for God's word as for food without which life cannot continue.

Every deliberate sin contains an element of pride.

God can silence liars.

Reproach and contempt may humble us and do us good before they are removed.

If the cross seems too heavy for us, the One who carried it for us can give us strength to carry it.

He will not let those upheld by him finally sink.

It is especially painful when people who should protect the innocent betray them.

The psalmist nevertheless continued in duty and found comfort in Scripture.

When other consolations become bitter, the Lord's word may become even sweeter to the believer.

To delight in God's testimonies, we must accept their guidance.

May he direct our repentance and our faith in Christ.

Repentance and an enlarged heart (verses 25–32)

Worldly-minded people cling to the earth as their ultimate possession.

Believers, by contrast, grieve over the remaining earthly desires within their own hearts.

It comforts them deeply to know how tenderly God receives their complaints.

We can speak of the wonders of redeeming love when we understand God's way and walk in it.

Repentance melts the heart with sorrow for sin.

Even a patient believer may be overcome by affliction and should then pour out the soul before God.

The way of falsehood includes every deceptive path—whether we deceive others, ourselves, or are misled by Satan and his agents.

Those who know and love God's law want to know it better and love it more.

The way of sincere godliness is the way of truth and the only true road to happiness.

We must take it seriously at every step.

Those who hold to God's word may pray in faith for acceptance.

Lord, do not let me act in a way that brings shame upon me, and do not reject my service.

Those journeying toward heaven must continue pressing forward.

God's Spirit enlarges the heart as he gives wisdom and freedom from sin.

Understanding God's law through his Spirit (verses 33–40)

Teach me your statutes, Lord—not merely their words, but how they apply to my life.

The Holy Spirit gives right understanding.

Having revelation written in Scripture is not enough unless the Spirit gives wisdom in the heart.

God puts his Spirit within believers and moves them to obey his statutes.

The psalmist prays particularly against covetousness.

To have the love of God rooted in our hearts, we must uproot the love of the world.

Friendship with the world is hostility toward God.

Give me new life in your way, so that I redeem my time and perform my duties eagerly.

Staring at empty attractions slows us down.

A traveler cannot reach the destination while stopping to inspect every passing sight.

God's promises assure believers of his preserving care.

When Satan persuades one of God's children to compromise with the world, he later reproaches that believer for the very fall he caused.

Victory comes through Christ's cross.

The sweetness of God's commands makes us want to know them more.

Where the Lord has given the will to obey, he will also provide the strength to act.

Freedom through obedience (verses 41–48)

Lord, faith has shown me your mercies.

Let prayer bring me to enjoy what you promised.

When the salvation of the saints is complete, everyone will see that trust in God's word was never wasted.

Pray that we will never be ashamed or afraid to acknowledge God's truth before other people.

The psalmist resolved to continue obeying, without turning back.

Serving sin is slavery. Serving God is freedom.

Complete happiness and genuine liberty cannot be separated from following the Lord's law.

We must openly confess our faith without fear or shame.

The more we delight in God's service, the more closely we approach the holiness for which we were created.

We should do more than approve the law as good.

We should enjoy it as good for us and exert our strength to follow it.

Something of this attitude of Christ belongs to every true disciple.

Remembering God's promises in adversity (verses 49–56)

Those who have made God's promises their portion may humbly yet boldly appeal to them.

The Spirit who creates faith within us will also act for us.

God's word gives comfort during suffering.

If it makes us holy through grace, it can sustain our peace in any condition.

Be sure that what you believe is genuinely taught by divine Scripture.

Then do not allow mockers to frighten you away from it.

God's earlier judgments comfort us because he remains the same.

Sin becomes hateful to those whom the Lord sanctifies.

Soon believers will be absent from the body and present with him.

Meanwhile his statutes give us constant reasons for praise.

During affliction and in the quiet hours of night, the psalmist remembered the Lord's name and returned to his commandments.

Everyone who has made true religion a priority will recognize how richly it has benefited them.

The Lord is my portion (verses 57–64)

Faithful believers choose the Lord as their inheritance.

Nothing less can satisfy them.

The psalmist prayed with his whole heart because he valued the blessing he requested.

He desired the promised mercy and depended upon God's promise to receive it.

He abandoned wrong paths and returned to the Lord's testimonies without delay.

Sinners should hurry to escape destruction, and believers should be equally eager to glorify God.

Neither anxiety nor sorrow should erase Scripture from our minds or rob us of its comfort.

There is no earthly situation in which a believer lacks reasons for thanksgiving.

We should be ashamed if others are more willing to lose sleep for sinful pleasures than we are to rise and praise the Lord.

Let us pray earnestly for hearts filled with mercy, grace and peace.

Affliction that teaches God's statutes (verses 65–72)

However God has treated us, he has treated us better than we deserve, acting in love for our ultimate good.

Many people have knowledge but little judgment.

Those with both are better prepared against Satan's traps and for God's service.

We are often most inclined to wander from the Lord when life is comfortable.

Because we do not know everything that is good for us, we should entrust our concerns to him.

Lord, you are a generous Benefactor.

Direct our hearts toward faith and obedience.

The psalmist resolved to continue faithfully and steadfastly.

Proud people become so filled with worldly riches and pleasures that they grow spiritually dull and careless.

God sometimes afflicts his people so they will learn his statutes.

Not only his promises but also his commands, however difficult they seem to unbelievers, are desirable and beneficial.

They guide us toward eternal life with safety and joy.

The compassion that sustains the upright (verses 73–80)

God created us to serve and enjoy him.

But our own sin has made us unfit to do either.

We must continually ask him, through the Holy Spirit, to give us understanding.

When other believers experience comfort from God, it should make us rejoice with them.

It is easy to say God's judgments are right until those judgments affect us personally.

Every support we receive during suffering comes from his mercy and compassion.

His mercies are tender.

They resemble a father's care and a mother's compassion for her child.

They come toward us even when we are unable to go toward them.

Groundless reproach does not truly harm us and should not divert us from duty.

The psalmist found comfort in continuing faithfully.

He prized the goodwill of fellow believers and desired fellowship with them.

An upright heart means sincere dependence upon God and wholehearted devotion to him.

Hope that continues when strength fails (verses 81–88)

The psalmist asked to be delivered from sin, enemies and fear.

Waiting for salvation made him weary; his eyes had grown tired looking for relief.

Yet when our eyes fail, faith must not fail.

His suffering was severe.

He compared himself to a leather bottle hung in smoke, dried out and shriveled.

Even then, we should remember God's statutes.

The days of believers' mourning will end; beside eternity, those days are brief.

Their enemies use cunning as well as strength, despising God's law.

But his commands remain reliable guides toward peace and safety.

We can especially hope for God's help when, like our Master, we do good and suffer because of it.

Wicked people may nearly destroy the believer on earth, but the believer would rather abandon everything else than abandon the Lord's word.

For every good work we depend upon divine grace.

The surest sign that God favors us is his good work within us.

God's word stands forever (verses 89–96)

The permanence of God's word in heaven stands against the changes and revolutions of the earth.

His covenant is established more firmly than the earth itself.

All created things fulfill the purposes for which they were made.

Should humanity, uniquely endowed with reason, become the one unprofitable burden upon creation?

Scripture can be our pleasant companion at any hour.

Yet the written word will not give spiritual life without God's grace.

The best aid for imperfect memory is strong affection.

Even if we forget the exact words, remembering their true meaning is valuable.

I belong to you, Lord—not to myself or the world.

Save me from sin and ruin.

God gives peace to the person whose mind remains fixed on him.

The perfections of this world all have limits and eventually fade like grass.

But God's word is complete and sufficient for every age and every situation.

It leads us away from confidence in human wisdom, strength and righteousness, directing us to seek happiness and comfort in Christ alone.

Loving and meditating on Scripture (verses 97–104)

We naturally think often about what we love.

All true wisdom comes from God.

A faithful believer carries the Bible everywhere—not necessarily in the hand, but in mind and heart.

Meditating on Scripture can give us deeper understanding than respected teachers possess, particularly when we learn to understand our own hearts.

The written word is a more reliable guide to heaven than all the fathers, teachers and ancient authorities of the church.

We cannot confidently approach God in worship while knowingly clinging to guilt or walking along sinful paths.

Divine grace enabled the psalmist to receive the Lord's instruction.

The soul has tastes and appetites, just as the body does.

Our delight in God's word grows as our appetite for worldly and fleshly pleasures diminishes.

Every path of sin is wrong.

The better we understand God's commands, the more deeply we hate sin.

And the better we know Scripture, the better equipped we become to answer temptation.

A lamp for every step (verses 105–112)

God's word directs our work and our path.

Without it, this world would be terribly dark.

His commandments are like a lamp, kept burning by the oil of the Spirit.

They guide both our choice of direction and the steps we take along it.

This obedience belongs to a sinner living under mercy and a believer who shares in the covenant of grace.

Though frequently afflicted, the psalmist continued longing for holiness and praying daily for life-giving grace.

Nothing we offer to God is acceptable unless he first teaches us how to offer it.

Holding our life continually in our hands means living under constant danger.

Yet the psalmist did not forget God's promises or commandments.

Wicked people set countless traps.

Blessed is the servant whom those traps do not turn away from the Master's way.

Heavenly treasures are an everlasting inheritance.

Those who value them can be content with little wealth on earth.

Comfort is found in the way of duty faithfully performed.

Through grace, a godly person brings the heart fully into the work and performs it well.

Watching against the first movements of sin (verses 113–120)

The psalmist feared even the first beginnings of sinful desire.

The more we love God's law, the more carefully we guard against empty thoughts that would draw us away.

To progress in obedience, we must separate ourselves from the influence of evildoers.

Believers cannot live spiritually without grace.

But when God's hand supports them, their spiritual life is preserved.

Their security rests upon divine help.

Departing from the Lord's statutes is error that leads toward destruction.

Wicked people's clever schemes are ultimately deceitful.

A day is coming when the wicked will face everlasting fire, the fitting place for dross.

Considering sin's consequences, we should fear coming short of the promised heavenly rest (Hebrews 4:1).

Justice, grace and Christ our Surety (verses 121–128)

Happy are those who practice justice toward others from gospel principles.

Christ our Surety has paid the debt and ransom of his people and secured all the blessings of salvation for genuine believers.

The psalmist expected the fulfillment of God's righteous word.

He looked for no salvation beyond what God had promised.

That word cannot fail.

We deserve no favor from God.

Our hearts find most rest when we entrust ourselves entirely to his mercy.

Those resolved to obey as God's servants will be taught his testimonies.

We should do everything within our power to support true religion, then ask God to take the work into his own hands.

Claiming to love his commandments more than our earthly interests is hypocrisy if our conduct proves otherwise.

The path of sin is a false path because it contradicts God's righteous commands.

Those who truly value his law hate sin and refuse to make peace with it.

Tears over disobedience (verses 129–136)

The wonders of redeeming love should fill our hearts with reverent admiration.

Scripture shows us what we were, what we are, and what we shall become.

It reveals God's mercy and justice, heaven's joy and hell's suffering.

In a short time, even people without advanced education can learn from it truths that philosophers searched for over many centuries.

Believers tired by the cares of life and the struggle against sin long for the comfort God's word supplies.

Everyone may pray: Look upon me and show me mercy, as you do to those who love your name.

Ask the Holy Spirit to direct every step.

We should fear sin's domination and earnestly pray against it.

Human oppression may become more than we can endure in our own strength.

The God who knows our frame can remove that pressure in answer to prayer.

Henry argues that the ancient Israelites' confidence in approaching God's throne indicates they understood more of gospel blessings through sacrifices and worship than people often suppose.

We should approach the same gracious throne through the name and merit of Jesus. We will not, and cannot, plead there in vain.

Those whose hearts have been transformed by grace often express that grace in tears.

Lord, receive the tears our blessed Redeemer shed for us during his earthly life, and teach us also to grieve over our own sins and the suffering of others.

God's righteousness and Christ's obedience (verses 137–144)

God has never done and never can do anything unjust.

He fulfills every promise faithfully.

Zeal against sin should make us act against it, beginning with greater faithfulness in our own lives.

Love for Scripture demonstrates love for God because it aims to make us participants in his holiness.

Genuine excellence makes people humble in their own eyes.

When we are overlooked or despised, we especially need to remember God's commands for encouragement.

His law is truth, the standard of holiness and the rule of happiness.

Yet only Christ's obedience justifies the believer.

Even saints experience sorrow and many trials.

Sometimes they taste the sweetness of God's word most deeply when suffering and distress surround them.

Eternal life is to know the only true God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent (John 17:3).

May we live now by faith and grace, then enter the life of glory.

Seeking the Lord morning and night (verses 145–152)

Wholehearted prayer belongs to people who truly desire God's salvation and love his commandments.

Where should a child go but to the Father?

Lord, save me from my sins, corruptions, temptations and everything that hinders obedience.

Christians who have good health should not waste the early hours of morning.

Hope in God's promises encourages us to keep praying.

It is better to give up some sleep than to find no time for prayer.

We may approach God at every hour.

When our first thoughts in the morning turn to him, we are better prepared to live in his fear throughout the day.

Ask him to give life, joy and cheerfulness.

He knows our needs and what is good for us.

When we are engaged in his service, we need not fear those who place themselves as far as possible from the commands of his word.

When trouble comes near, God is also near.

All his commandments are true, and all his promises will be fulfilled.

Everyone who has trusted him has found him faithful.

The living word and the inexhaustible mercy of God (verses 153–160)

The more closely we hold God's word as both our rule and our support, the stronger our confidence in deliverance.

Christ is the Redeemer and Advocate of his people.

Those whom the Spirit once made alive when they were dead in sins still need fresh grace to revive them according to God's promises.

The wicked do not obey God's statutes; they do not even seek to know them.

They flatter themselves that they are traveling toward heaven.

But as long as they continue in sin, they move further from it.

God's tender mercies are a fountain that never runs dry.

The psalmist begged for renewed life-giving grace.

Someone steadily performing duty need not fear numerous enemies.

Those who truly hate sin hate it because it violates God's law and breaks his word, not merely because it is inconvenient.

Obedience is pleasing to God and joyful to us only when it springs from love.

In every age, everyone who receives Scripture with faith and love discovers that every word of it is faithful.

Great peace through love for God's law (verses 161–168)

Those who stand in awe of God's word will endure human anger rather than break his commandments.

Through Scripture we receive immeasurable benefit.

Everyone dislikes being lied to.

But we should hate telling lies even more, because that insults God directly.

The more we love truth's beauty, the more we recognize the ugliness of falsehood.

We should praise God even for trials, because his grace can use them for our good.

People who love this world experience great unrest because it disappoints them.

Those who love God's word find great peace, because it exceeds their expectations.

Genuine love for the Lord keeps us from unnecessary doubts and from constantly taking offense at other believers.

A sound hope of salvation motivates us to obey.

Our love for Scripture must also weaken sinful desires and uproot fleshly attachments.

It must engage the heart, or it accomplishes nothing.

We keep God's commands through obedience, and keep his promises through reliance upon them.

God sees us continually.

That should make us careful in all our conduct.

Seek me and give me life (verses 169–176)

The psalmist asked for the grace and strength needed to pray, and for God to receive his petitions.

He wanted to know more of God in Christ, to understand Scripture's teachings and carry out his duties.

He knew his unworthiness and approached with reverent concern.

He appealed to what God had promised, not to his own merit.

We have not truly learned from God unless we have learned to praise him.

His word must govern our speech.

We must avoid both sinful speaking and sinful silence.

Our hands are insufficient, and no creature can provide all the help we need.

We look to the One who made us for support.

The psalmist had deliberately chosen to follow God.

Every saint longs for eternal salvation and therefore prays for help along the way.

May all God's ordinances and providential dealings advance his glory in our lives.

The believer looks back with both shame and thankfulness on being lost.

Still needing tender care, we pray to the Shepherd who purchased his flock with his own blood and grants eternal life.

Seek me means find me.

God never seeks in vain.

Turn me, Lord, and I shall be turned.

Let this psalm examine our hearts and lives.

Do our hearts, washed in Christ's blood, truly make its prayers, promises and confessions our own?

Is the Lord's word the standard of what we believe and how we live?

Do we plead its promises before Christ for what we need?

Happy are those who find delight in living this way.
classic_reading:
[Ps.119.1-Ps.119.8]
Chapter 119
The general scope and design of this psalm is to magnify the Divine law, and make it honourable. There are ten words by which Divine revelation is called in this psalm, and each expresses what God expects from us, and what we may expect from him. 1. God's law; this is enacted by him as our Sovereign. 2. His way; this is the rule of his providence. 3. His testimonies; they are solemnly declared to the world. 4. His commandments; given with authority. 5. His precepts; not left as indifferent matters to us. 6. His word, or saying; it is the declaration of his mind. 7. His judgments; framed in infinite wisdom. 8. His righteousness; it is the rule and standard of what is right. 9. His statutes; they are always binding. 10. His truth or faithfulness; it is eternal truth, it shall endure for ever.
Verses 1-8
This psalm may be considered as the statement of a believer's experience. As far as our views, desires, and affections agree with what is here expressed, they come from the influences of the Holy Spirit, and no further. The pardoning mercy of God in Christ, is the only source of a sinner's happiness. And those are most happy, who are preserved most free from the defilement of sin, who simply believe God's testimonies, and depend on his promises. If the heart be divided between him and the world, it is evil. But the saints carefully avoid all sin; they are conscious of much evil that clogs them in the ways of God, but not of that wickedness which draws them out of those ways. The tempter would make men think they are at them out of those ways. The tempter would make men think they are at liberty to follow the word of God or not, as they please. But the desire and prayer of a good man agree with the will and command of God. If a man expects by obedience in one thing to purchase indulgence for disobedience in others, his hypocrisy will be detected; if he is not ashamed in this world, everlasting shame will be his portion. The psalmist coveted to learn the laws of God, to give God the glory. And believers see that if God forsakes them, the temper will be too hard for them.
[Ps.119.9-Ps.119.16]
Verses 9-16
To original corruption all have added actual sin. The ruin of the young is either living by no rule at all, or choosing false rules: let them walk by Scripture rules. To doubt of our own wisdom and strength, and to depend upon God, proves the purpose of holiness is sincere. God's word is treasure worth laying up, and there is no laying it up safe but in our hearts, that we may oppose God's precepts to the dominion of sin, his promises to its allurements, and his threatenings to its violence. Let this be our plea with Him to teach us his statutes, that, being partakers of his holiness, we may also partake of his blessedness. And those whose hearts are fed with the bread of life, should with their lips feed many. In the way of God's commandments there is the unsearchable riches of Christ. But we do not meditate on God's precepts to good purpose, unless our good thoughts produce good works. I will not only think of thy statutes, but do them with delight. And it will be well to try the sincerity of our obedience by tracing the spring of it; the reality of our love by cheerfulness in appointed duties.
[Ps.119.17-Ps.119.24]
Verses 17-24
If God deals in strict justice with us, we all perish. We ought to spend our lives in his service; we shall find true life in keeping his word. Those that would see the wondrous things of God's law and gospel, must beg him to give them understanding, by the light of his Spirit. Believers feel themselves strangers on earth; they fear missing their way, and losing comfort by erring from God's commandments. Every sanctified soul hungers after the word of God, as food which there is no living without. There is something of pride at the bottom of every wilful sin. God can silence lying lips; reproach and contempt may humble and do us good, and then they shall be removed. Do we find the weight of the cross is above that we are able to bear? He that bore it for us will enable us to bear it; upheld by him we cannot sink. It is sad when those who should protect the innocent, are their betrayers. The psalmist went on in duty, and he found comfort in the word of God. The comforts of the word of God are most pleasant to a gracious soul, when other comforts are made bitter; and those that would have God's testimonies to be their delight, must be advised by them. May the Lord direct us in exercising repentance of sin, and faith in Christ.
[Ps.119.25-Ps.119.32]
Verses 25-32
While the souls of the children of this world cleave to the earth as their portion, the children of light are greatly burdened, because of the remains of carnal affections in their hearts. It is unspeakable comfort to a gracious soul, to think with what tenderness all its complaints are received by a gracious God. We can talk of the wonders of redeeming love, when we understand the way of God's precepts, and walk in that way. The penitent melts in sorrow for sin: even the patient spirit may melt in the sense of affliction, it is then its interest to pour out its soul before God. The way of lying means all false ways by which men deceive themselves and others, or are deceived by Satan and his instruments. Those who know and love the law of the Lord, desire to know it more, and love it better. The way of serious godliness is the way of truth; the only true way to happiness: we must always have actual regard to it. Those who stick to the word of God, may in faith expect and pray for acceptance with God. Lord, never leave me to do that by which I shall shame myself, and do not thou reject my services. Those that are going to heaven, should still press forward. God, by his Spirit, enlarges the hearts of his people when he gives them wisdom. The believer prays to be set free from sin.
[Ps.119.33-Ps.119.40]
Verses 33-40
Teach me thy statutes, not the mere words, but the way of applying them to myself. God, by his Spirit, gives a right understanding. But the Spirit of revelation in the word will not suffice, unless we have the Spirit of wisdom in the heart. God puts his Spirit within us, causing us to walk in his statutes. The sin here prayed against is covetousness. Those that would have the love of God rooted in them, must get the love of the world rooted out; for the friendship of the world is enmity with God. Quicken me in thy way; to redeem time, and to do every duty with liveliness of spirit. Beholding vanity deadens us, and slackens our pace; a traveller must not stand gazing upon every object that presents itself to his view. The promises of God's word greatly relate to the preservation of the true believer. When Satan has drawn a child of God into worldly compliances, he will reproach him with the falls into which he led him. Victory must come from the cross of Christ. When we enjoy the sweetness of God's precepts, it will make us long for more acquaintance with them. And where God has wrought to will, he will work to do.
[Ps.119.41-Ps.119.48]
Verses 41-48
Lord, I have by faith thy mercies in view; let me by prayer prevail to obtain them. And when the salvation of the saints is completed, it will plainly appear that it was not in vain to trust in God's word. We need to pray that we may never be afraid or ashamed to own God's truths and ways before men. And the psalmist resolves to keep God's law, in a constant course of obedience, without backsliding. The service of sin is slavery; the service of God is liberty. There is no full happiness, or perfect liberty, but in keeping God's law. We must never be ashamed or afraid to own our religion. The more delight we take in the service of God, the nearer we come to perfection. Not only consent to his law as good, but take pleasure in it as good for us. Let me put forth all the strength I have, to do it. Something of this mind of Christ is in every true disciple.
[Ps.119.49-Ps.119.56]
Verses 49-56
Those that make God's promises their portion, may with humble boldness make them their plea. He that by his Spirit works faith in us, will work for us. The word of God speaks comfort in affliction. If, through grace, it makes us holy, there is enough in it to make us easy, in all conditions. Let us be certain we have the Divine law for what we believe, and then let not scoffers prevail upon us to decline from it. God's judgments of old comfort and encourage us, for he is still the same. Sin is horrible in the eyes of all that are sanctified. Ere long the believer will be absent from the body, and present with the Lord. In the mean time, the statutes of the Lord supply subjects for grateful praise. In the season of affliction, and in the silent hours of the night, he remembers the name of the Lord, and is stirred up to keep the law. All who have made religion the first thing, will own that they have been unspeakable gainers by it.
[Ps.119.57-Ps.119.64]
Verses 57-64
True believers take the Lord for the portion of their inheritance, and nothing less will satisfy them. The psalmist prayed with his whole heart, knowing how to value the blessing he prayed for: he desired the mercy promised, and depended on the promise for it. He turned from by-paths, and returned to God's testimonies. He delayed not. It behoves sinners to hasten to escape; and the believer will be equally in haste to glorify God. No care or grief should take away God's word out of our minds, or hinder the comfort it bestows. There is no situation on earth in which a believer has not cause to be thankful. Let us feel ashamed that others are more willing to keep from sleep to spend the time in sinful pleasures, than we are to praise God. And we should be more earnest in prayer, that our hearts may be filled with his mercy, grace, and peace.
[Ps.119.65-Ps.119.72]
Verses 65-72
However God has dealt with us, he has dealt with us better than we deserve; and all in love, and for our good. Many have knowledge, but little judgment; those who have both, are fortified against the snares of Satan, and furnished for the service of God. We are most apt to wander from God, when we are easy in the world. We should leave our concerns to the disposal of God, seeing we know not what is good for us. Lord, thou art our bountiful Benefactor; incline our hearts to faith and obedience. The psalmist will go on in his duty with constancy and resolution. The proud are full of the world, and its wealth and pleasures; these make them senseless, secure, and stupid. God visits his people with affliction, that they may learn his statutes. Not only God's promises, but even his law, his percepts, though hard to ungodly men, are desirable, and profitable, because they lead us with safety and delight unto eternal life.
[Ps.119.73-Ps.119.80]
Verses 73-80
God made us to serve him, and enjoy him; but by sin we have made ourselves unfit to serve him, and to enjoy him. We ought, therefore, continually to beseech him, by his Holy Spirit, to give us understanding. The comforts some have in God, should be matter of joy to others. But it is easy to own, that God's judgments are right, until it comes to be our own case. All supports under affliction must come from mercy and compassion. The mercies of God are tender mercies; the mercies of a father, the compassion of a mother to her son. They come to us when we are not able to go to them. Causeless reproach does not hurt, and should not move us. The psalmist could go on in the way of his duty, and find comfort in it. He valued the good will of saints, and was desirous to keep up his communion with them. Soundness of heart signifies sincerity in dependence on God, and devotedness to him.
[Ps.119.81-Ps.119.88]
Verses 81-88
The psalmist sought deliverance from his sins, his foes, and his fears. Hope deferred made him faint; his eyes failed by looking out for this expected salvation. But when the eyes fail, yet faith must not. His affliction was great. He was become like a leathern bottle, which, if hung up in the smoke, is dried and shrivelled up. We must ever be mindful of God's statutes. The days of the believer's mourning shall be ended; they are but for a moment, compared with eternal happiness. His enemies used craft as well as power for his ruin, in contempt of the law of God. The commandments of God are true and faithful guides in the path of peace and safety. We may best expect help from God when, like our Master, we do well and suffer for it. Wicked men may almost consume the believer upon earth, but he would sooner forsake all than forsake the word of the Lord. We should depend upon the grace of God for strength to do every good work. The surest token of God's good-will toward us, is his good work in us.
[Ps.119.89-Ps.119.96]
Verses 89-96
The settling of God's word in heaven, is opposed to the changes and revolutions of the earth. And the engagements of God's covenant are established more firmly than the earth itself. All the creatures answer the ends of their creation: shall man, who alone is endued with reason, be the only unprofitable burden of the earth? We may make the Bible a pleasant companion at any time. But the word, without the grace of God, would not quicken us. See the best help for bad memories, namely, good affections; and though the exact words be lost, if the meaning remain, that is well. I am thine, not my own, not the world's; save me from sin, save me from ruin. The Lord will keep the man in peace, whose mind is stayed on him. It is poor perfection which one sees and end of. Such are all things in this world, which pass for perfections. The glory of man is but as the flower of the grass. The psalmist had seen the fulness of the word of God, and its sufficiency. The word of the Lord reaches to all cases, to all times. It will take us from all confidence in man, or in our own wisdom, strength, and righteousness. Thus shall we seek comfort and happiness from Christ alone.
[Ps.119.97-Ps.119.104]
Verses 97-104
What we love, we love to think of. All true wisdom is from God. A good man carries his Bible with him, if not in his hands, yet in his head and in his heart. By meditation on God's testimonies we understand more than our teachers, when we understand our own hearts. The written word is a more sure guide to heaven, than all the fathers, the teachers, and ancients of the church. We cannot, with any comfort or boldness, attend God in holy duties, while under guilt, or in any by-way. It was Divine grace in his heart, that enabled the psalmist to receive these instructions. The soul has its tastes as well as the body. Our relish for the word of God will be greatest, when that for the world and the flesh is least. The way of sin is a wrong way; and the more understanding we get by the precepts of God, the more rooted will be our hatred of sin; and the more ready we are in the Scriptures, the better furnished we are with answers to temptation.
[Ps.119.105-Ps.119.112]
Verses 105-112
The word of God directs us in our work and way, and a dark place indeed the world would be without it. The commandment is a lamp kept burning with the oil of the Spirit, as a light to direct us in the choice of our way, and the steps we take in that way. The keeping of God's commands here meant, was that of a sinner under a dispensation of mercy, of a believer having part in the covenant of grace. The psalmist is often afflicted; but with longing desires to become more holy, offers up daily prayers for quickening grace. We cannot offer any thing to God, that he will accept but what he is pleased to teach us to do. To have our soul or life continually in our hands, implies constant danger of life; yet he did not forget God's promises nor his precepts. Numberless are the snares laid by the wicked; and happy is that servant of God, whom they have not caused to err from his Master's precepts. Heavenly treasures are a heritage for ever; all the saints accept them as such, therefore they can be content with little of this world. We must look for comfort only in the way of duty, and that duty must be done. A good man, by the grace of God, brings his heart to his work, then it is done well.
[Ps.119.113-Ps.119.120]
Verses 113-120
Here is a dread of the risings of sin, and the first beginnings of it. The more we love the law of God, the more watchful we shall be, lest vain thoughts draw us from what we love. Would we make progress in keeping God's commands, we must be separate from evil-doers. The believer could not live without the grace of God; but, supported by his hand, his spiritual life shall be maintained. Our holy security is grounded on Divine supports. All departure from God's statutes is error, and will prove fatal. Their cunning is falsehood. There is a day coming which will put the wicked into everlasting fire, the fit place for the dross. See what comes of sin Surely we who fall so low in devout affections, should fear, lest a promise being left us of entering into heavenly rest, any of us should be found to come short of it, [Heb.4.1] He 4:1.
[Ps.119.121-Ps.119.128]
Verses 121-128
Happy is the man, who, acting upon gospel principles, does justice to all around. Christ our Surety, having paid our debt and ransom, secures all the blessings of salvation to every true believer. The psalmist expects the word of God's righteousness, and no other salvation than what is secured by that word, which cannot fall to the ground. We deserve no favour form God; we are most easy when we cast ourselves upon God's mercy, and refer ourselves to it. If any man resolve to do God's will as his servant, he shall be made to know his testimonies. We must do what we can for the support of religion, and, after all, must beg of God to take the work into his own hands. It is hypocrisy to say we love God's commandments more than our worldly interests. The way of sin is a false way, being directly contrary to God's precepts, which are right: those that love and esteem God's law, hate sin, and will not be reconciled to it.
[Ps.119.129-Ps.119.136]
Verses 129-136
The wonders of redeeming love will fix the heart in adoration of them. The Scriptures show us what we were, what we are, and what we shall be. They show us the mercy and the justice of the Lord, the joys of heaven, and the pains of hell. Thus they give to the simple, in a few days, understanding of those matters, which philosophers for ages sought in vain. The believer, wearied with the cares of life and his conflicts with sin, pants for the consolations conveyed to him by means of the sacred word. And every one may pray, Look thou upon me, and be merciful unto me as thou usest to do unto those that love thy name. We must beg that the Holy Spirit would order our steps. The dominion of sin is to be dreaded and prayed against by every one. The oppression of men is often more than flesh and blood can bear; and He who knoweth our frame, will not refuse to remove it in answer to the prayers of his people. Whatever obscurity may appear as to the faith of the Old Testament believers, their confidence at the throne of grace can only be explained by their having obtained more distinct views of gospel privileges, through the sacrifices and services of their law, than is generally imagined. Go to the same place, plead the name and merits of Jesus, and you will not, you cannot plead in vain. Commonly, where there is a gracious heart, there is a weeping eye. Accept, O Lord, the tears our blessed Redeemer shed in the days of his flesh, for us who should weep for our brethren or ourselves.
[Ps.119.137-Ps.119.144]
Verses 137-144
God never did, and never can do wrong to any. The promises are faithfully performed by Him that made them. Zeal against sin should constrain us to do what we can against it, at least to do more in religion ourselves. Our love to the word of God is evidence of our love to God, because it is designed to make us partake his holiness. Men's real excellency always makes them low in their own eyes. When we are small and despised, we have the more need to remember God's precepts, that we may have them to support us. The law of God is the truth, the standard of holiness, the rule of happiness; but the obedience of Christ alone justifies the believer. Sorrows are often the lot of saints in this vale of tears; they are in heaviness through manifold temptations. There are delights in the word of God, which the saints often most sweetly enjoy when in trouble and anguish. This is life eternal, to know God and Jesus Christ whom he has sent, [John.17.3] Joh 17:3. May we live the life of faith and grace here, and be removed to the life of glory hereafter.
[Ps.119.145-Ps.119.152]
Verses 145-152
Supplications with the whole heart are presented only by those who desire God's salvation, and who love his commandments. Whither should the child go but to his father? Save me from my sins, my corruptions, my temptations, all the hinderances in my way, that I may keep thy testimonies. Christians who enjoy health, should not suffer the early hours of the morning to glide away unimproved. Hope in God's word encourages us to continue in prayer. It is better to take time from sleep, than not to find time for prayer. We have access to God at all hours; and if our first thoughts in the morning are of God, they will help to keep us in his fear all the day long. Make me lively and cheerful. God knows what we need and what is good for us, and will quicken us. If we are employed in God's service, we need not fear those who try to set themselves as far as they can out of the reach of the convictions and commands of his law. When trouble is near, God is near. He is never far to seek. All his commandments are truth. And God's promises will be performed. All that ever trusted in God have found him faithful.
[Ps.119.153-Ps.119.160]
Verses 153-160
The closer we cleave to the word of God, both as our rule and as our stay, the more assurance we have of deliverance. Christ is the Advocate of his people, their Redeemer. Those who were quickened by his Spirit and grace, when they were dead in trespasses and sins, often need to have the work of grace revived in them, according to the word of promise. The wicked not only do not God's statutes, but they do not even seek them. They flatter themselves that they are going to heaven; but the longer they persist in sin, the further it is from them. God's mercies are tender; they are a fountain that can never be exhausted. The psalmist begs for God's reviving, quickening grace. A man, steady in the way of his duty, though he may have many enemies, needs to fear none. Those that hate sin truly, hate it as sin, as a transgression of the law of God, and a breaking of his word. Our obedience is only pleasing to God, and pleasant to ourselves, when it comes from a principle of love. All, in every age, who receive God's word in faith and love, find every saying in it faithful.
[Ps.119.161-Ps.119.168]
Verses 161-168
Those whose hearts stand in awe of God's word, will rather endure the wrath of man, than break the law of God. By the word of God we are unspeakable gainers. Every man hates to have a lie told him, but we should more hate telling a lie; by the latter we give an affront to God. The more we see the beauty of truth, the more we shall see the hateful deformity of a lie. We are to praise God even for afflictions; through grace we get good from them. Those that love the world have great vexation, for it does not answer what they expect; those that love God's word have great peace, for it outdoes what they expect. Those in whom this holy love reigns, will not perplex themselves with needless scruples, or take offence at their brethren. A good hope of salvation will engage the heart in doing the commandments. And our love to the word of God must subdue our lusts, and root out carnal affections: we must make heart work of it, or we make nothing of it. We must keep the commandments of God by obedience to them, and his promises by reliance on them. God's eye is on us at all times; this should make us very careful to keep his commandments.
[Ps.119.169-Ps.119.176]
Verses 169-176
The psalmist desired grace and strength to lift up his prayers, and that the Lord would receive and notice them. He desired to know more of God in Christ; to know more of the doctrines of the word, and the duties of religion. He had a deep sense of unworthiness, and holy fear that his prayer should not come before God; Lord, what I pray for is, what thou hast promised. We have learned nothing to purpose, if we have not learned to praise God. We should always make the word of God the rule of our discourse, so as never to transgress it by sinful speaking, or sinful silence. His own hands are not sufficient, nor can any creature lend him help; therefore he looks up to God, that the hand that had made him may help him. He had made religion his deliberate choice. There is an eternal salvation all the saints long for, and therefore they pray that God would help their way to it. Let thy judgments help me; let all ordinances and all providences, (both are God's judgments,) further me in glorifying God; let them help me for that work. He often looks back with shame and gratitude to his lost estate. He still prays for the tender care of Him who purchased his flock with his own blood, that he may receive from him the gift of eternal life. Seek me, that is, Find me; for God never seeks in vain. Turn me, and I shall be turned. Let this psalm be a touchstone by which to try our hearts, and our lives. Do our hearts, cleansed in Christ's blood, make these prayers, resolutions and confessions our own? Is God's word the standard of our faith, and the law of our practice? Do we use it as pleas with Christ for what we need? Happy those who live in such delightful exercises.

[Ps.120.1-Ps.120.4]
Chapter 120
Chapter Outline
The psalmist prays to God to deliver him from false and malicious tongues. | (1-4) |
He complains of wicked neighbours. | (5-7) |
Verses 1-4
The psalmist was brought into great distress by a deceitful tongue. May every good man be delivered from lying lips. They forged false charges against him. In this distress, he sought God by fervent prayer. God can bridle their tongues. He obtained a gracious answer to this prayer. Surely sinners durst not act as they do, if they knew, and would be persuaded to think, what will be in the end thereof. The terrors of the Lord are his arrows; and his wrath is compared to burning coals of juniper, which have a fierce heat, and keep fire very long. This is the portion of the false tongue; for all that love and make a lie, shall have their portion in the lake that burns eternally.
[Ps.120.5-Ps.120.7]
Verses 5-7
It is very grievous to a good man, to be cast into, and kept in the company of the wicked, from whom he hopes to be for ever separated. See here the character of a good man; he is for living peaceably with all men. And let us follow David as he prefigured Christ; in our distress let us cry unto the Lord, and he will hear us. Let us follow after peace and holiness, striving to overcome evil with good.
